prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I have two monuments besides this granite obelisk: One, the house I built on the hill, With its spires, bay windows, and roof of slate; The other, the lake-front in Chicago, Where the railroad keeps a switching yard, With whistling engines and crunching wheels, And smoke and soot thrown over the city, And the crash of cars along the boulevard, i A blot like a hog-pen on the harbor Of a great metropolis, foul as a sty. I helped to give this heritage To generations yet unborn, with my vote In the House of Representatives, And the lure of the thing was to be at rest From the never-ending fright of need, And to give my daughters gentle breeding, And a sense of security in life. But, you see, though I had the mansion house And traveling passes and local distinction, I could hear the whispers, whispers, whispers, Wherever I went, and my daughters grew up With a look as if some one were about to strike them; And they married madly, helter-skelter, Just to get out and have a change. And what was the whole of the business worth? Why, it wasn't worth a damn!

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: One, With, The

outputs.L1:
I have two monuments besides this granite obelisk:  
One is the house I built upon the hill,  
with its spires, bay windows, and slate roof;  
the other is the lakefront in Chicago,  
where the railroad maintains a switching yard,  
with whistling engines and grinding wheels,  
smoke and soot cast over the city,  
and the crash of cars along the boulevard—  
a blot, like a hog pen upon the harbor  
of a great metropolis, foul as a sty.

I helped bequeath this heritage  
to generations yet unborn, by my vote  
in the House of Representatives.  
And the lure of it all was the hope of rest  
from the unending terror of need,  
and the desire to give my daughters gentle breeding  
and a sense of security in life.

But you see, though I had the mansion,  
the travel passes, and local distinction,  
I could hear the whispers—whispers, whispers—  
wherever I went. And my daughters grew up  
with a look as though someone were about to strike them;  
and they married recklessly, helter-skelter,  
just to escape and find a change.

And what was the whole affair worth?  
Why, it wasn’t worth a damn.
outputs.L2:
Beyond this granite obelisk, I leave behind two other memorials.

The first is the home I constructed on the hill,  
with its towers, projecting windows, and slate-covered roof.

The second is Chicago’s lakefront,  
where the railroad maintains its switching yard—  
engines shrieking, wheels grinding,  
smoke and grime spreading across the city,  
railcars clattering along the boulevard—  
an ugly stain on the harbor  
of a major city, filthy as a pigsty.

I helped pass this legacy on  
to people not yet born,  
through the vote I cast  
in the House of Representatives.

What tempted me was the hope of peace:  
freedom from the constant terror of poverty,  
the chance to raise my daughters with refinement,  
and the feeling that life would be safe and secure.

But even though I had the grand house,  
the railroad passes, and the respect of the town,  
I still heard murmuring everywhere—  
whispers, always whispers.

My daughters grew up wearing an expression  
as though they expected someone to hit them at any moment.  
Then they rushed into marriages wildly and recklessly,  
only to escape and find some kind of change.

And in the end, what was all of it worth?  
Nothing at all.
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents three “monuments” to his legacy, each representing a different aspect of his life and moral compromise. The first is a granite obelisk, a formal memorial meant to preserve his name after death. The second is a grand house on a hill, a symbol of the wealth, status, and comfort he achieved during his lifetime. The third, and most troubling, is the polluted Chicago lake-front, scarred and shaped by railroad development. Unlike the obelisk and the house, this monument is not honorable or beautiful; it is a public reminder of the damage caused by political corruption and private ambition.

The speaker admits that he helped create this blighted lake-front through his vote in the House of Representatives. By supporting railroad interests, he contributed to the transformation of the shoreline into something degraded and industrialized. His action was not simply a matter of public policy; it was part of a personal bargain. He used his political power in a way that benefited himself and helped secure the future he desired for his family.

His motive, however, was not presented as simple greed. He explains that he wanted to escape poverty and protect himself from the insecurity of want. He longed for comfort, respectability, and a life free from hardship. More importantly, he wanted to provide his daughters with refinement, safety, and social advantage. In his mind, the compromises he made were justified because they would give his family opportunities and protection that he had never known.

Yet the rewards he gained did not bring peace. Although he acquired wealth, social position, and the privileges that came with influence, he remained haunted by the judgment of others. Public whispers followed him, and the shame of his choices could not be erased by money or status. The outward signs of success only made the inner disgrace more painful, because they stood as reminders of what he had sacrificed to obtain them.

The deepest irony is that the very daughters he hoped to protect suffered because of the family’s disgrace. Instead of enjoying the refined and secure life he had imagined for them, they were burdened by his compromised reputation. Feeling trapped by public shame, they rushed into marriages as a way to escape the shadow of the family name. In the end, the speaker is left with a bitter conclusion: the wealth and comfort he gained were worthless. His compromises did not save his family or secure their happiness. They produced only monuments to ambition, corruption, and regret.
outputs.L4:
The speaker looks back on the “monuments” he has left behind and recognizes that they are not noble achievements but signs of moral failure. One monument is his grand house, built to display wealth, success, and social standing. The other is the ruined Chicago lakefront, where a switching yard was allowed to corrupt and disfigure public space. Both were created through political compromise: he made deals, accepted corruption, and helped private interests triumph over the public good.

He admits that his choices were driven less by principle than by fear. He feared poverty, obscurity, and the insecurity that might threaten his family. He wanted to protect his wife and children, give them comfort, and secure their place in society. At the time, the bargain may have seemed practical or even necessary. By cooperating with powerful men and surrendering his ideals, he gained money, distinction, influence, and a comfortable life.

Yet in retrospect, he sees that the cost was far greater than the reward. His wealth did not bring honor, and his public success did not bring peace. Instead, his compromise produced shame. His family, whom he hoped to protect, was damaged by the consequences of his actions and by the disgrace attached to his name. The city also suffered: the lakefront, which should have belonged to the people as a source of beauty and civic pride, was permanently harmed by greed and political corruption.

The speaker therefore judges his own life harshly. The house and the switching yard stand as monuments, but not to greatness. They represent fear, cowardice, and the surrender of public responsibility for private gain. Although he achieved the outward signs of success, he concludes that the bargain was morally worthless. What he gained in comfort and status was outweighed by public dishonor, injury to his family, and lasting damage to the community.
outputs.L5:
**One With The Moment**

One quiet morning, the world seemed to slow down. The sky was soft, the air was calm, and every sound felt gentle and clear. With each breath, there was a sense of peace that made everything feel simple and complete.

Sometimes, life moves so quickly that we forget to notice the small things around us. The warmth of sunlight, the sound of leaves, and the comfort of silence can all remind us to be present. With patience and attention, even an ordinary day can become meaningful.

To be One with the moment is to accept it fully. The past has already gone, and the future has not yet arrived. What remains is the present, waiting to be experienced with an open heart.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Edgar Lee Masters' Spoon River Anthology about a corrupt politician reflecting bitterly on his legacy.
counterfactuals.output:
**Silas Crane**

I was chairman of roads and bridges,  
keeper of licenses, friend of the bank,  
and the man who could make a summons vanish  
if the envelope came sealed and fat.

You called me “Honorable” in daylight,  
and “Silas” at the back door.  
You spat when I passed—  
but you came, every one of you,  
with your brother’s tax, your son’s indictment,  
your bid for the courthouse roof.

Do not carve “Thief” on my stone.  
Carve “Mirror.”  
For what did I take  
that was not first offered?  
What law did I bend  
that some good citizen did not beg me to break?

I paved the west road  
because Harlan’s quarry paid me.  
I kept the schoolhouse leaking  
because the board opposed me.  
I sent young Abel Price to prison  
and kept Judge Monroe’s nephew free—  
and afterward heard both mothers  
pray to the same God.

Now the reformers stand over me  
with clean hands folded,  
their mouths full of virtue.  
They have named a ditch for me—  
Crane Run—  
where spring rain carries tin cans,  
dead leaves, and the town’s black water  
past the cemetery wall.

This is my monument:  
not the granite angel my widow bought,  
but the whispers that fattened on me,  
the favors that outlived me,  
the men I made rich  
who cross the street from my grave.

And you, passerby,  
reading my name in the lichen—  
tell me:  
when your chance came quietly,  
wearing no devil’s horns,  
only a clerk’s smile  
and a key to a locked drawer,  
did you refuse?
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dramatic free-verse epitaph spoken by a dead congressman who traded his vote for wealth, status, and security, only to regret it.
counterfactuals.output:
Here I lie—  
beneath marble bought by the same hands  
that purchased my silence.

I was once a voice  
sent from the dust roads,  
the mill towns,  
the crowded kitchens where mothers counted coins  
like rosary beads  
and prayed I would remember them.

I remembered.

Then I learned the price of forgetting.

A dinner at midnight.  
A hand on my shoulder.  
A promise wrapped in velvet:  
security,  
influence,  
a name engraved on doors  
I had never been invited to enter.

And so I sold one vote—  
only one, I told myself,  
as though a soul can be pawned  
by the ounce.

The bill passed.  
The poor grew quieter.  
The rich grew kind to me.  
My children were admitted.  
My wife was admired.  
My enemies called me practical.  
My friends stopped calling.

I slept in guarded houses  
and woke to unguarded dreams:  
faces in factory light,  
farmers under auction signs,  
veterans waiting in corridors,  
all of them holding my ballot  
like a broken bone.

Do not praise me now.  
Do not carve “public servant”  
above the place where I rot.

Write this instead:

He feared losing everything  
except his honor,  
and so he lost that first.

Let the rain read it.  
Let the worms know.  
Let every young lawmaker passing by  
feel the cold beneath these stones  
and understand:

A vote is not a coin.  
A seat is not a throne.  
The people are not steps  
to climb into comfort.

I rose,  
I dined,  
I signed,  
I smiled for the cameras—

and when death came,  
it did not call me Congressman.

It called me debtor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Spoon River-style monologue mentioning a granite obelisk, a mansion on a hill, and a polluted Chicago lakefront railroad yard.
counterfactuals.output:
I was Jonas Bell,  
Who built the mansion on the hill  
With windows bright as courthouse eyes,  
And a lawn combed smooth by hired men.

You remember the granite obelisk—  
Tall, gray, respectable—  
Set above my grave by my children  
Who quarreled over the silver  
Before the mortar dried.

I began with a ledger and a lie,  
Buying lots where smoke blew east  
From the polluted Chicago lakefront railroad yard,  
Where the cinders settled on bread,  
And the lake took oil, sewage, and prayer  
In the same dull wave.

I called it progress.  
I called it enterprise.  
The men with blackened collars  
Called it work, when they were living,  
And judgment, when they coughed themselves here  
Under smaller stones than mine.

Now from this hill of the dead  
I can see more clearly  
Than I ever saw from my balcony:  
The mansion was only a lantern  
Hung over a swamp,  
The obelisk only a finger  
Pointing nowhere,  
And my name, cut deep in granite,  
Is weathering faster  
Than the faces of those I never paid.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a bleak early-20th-century American poem where the speaker confesses that his public achievements and family comforts were not worth the shame.
counterfactuals.output:
I stood on platforms under flags,  
and shook the great men by the hand;  
my name was printed, praised, and spelled  
in gold upon the town-house wall.  

I had a porch, a maple shade,  
a wife who kept the lamp alight,  
two children with their Sunday shoes,  
and silver paid for, piece by piece.  

The bank would bow when I came in.  
The judge would call me “friend.” At church  
they gave me pews near the front,  
where all could see how clean I was.  

But in the mill-yard, after dusk,  
men coughed blood into their sleeves.  
Their widows learned my office stairs.  
Their daughters passed me, eyes cast down.  

I signed the papers. I knew the rates.  
I knew what boards would break, and where.  
I knew the river carried black  
what should have been kept out of it.  

For every laurel on my door  
there was a face I would not meet;  
for every comfort in my house  
a silence sitting down to eat.  

O wife, your curtains, white as milk,  
were bought with winter in their rooms.  
O sons, your books and baseball gloves  
were paid for by another’s breath.  

And now the speeches turn to dust,  
the photographs grow brown with damp;  
my medals sleep in a bureau drawer  
like coins left on a dead man’s eyes.  

I tell you from this narrow bed,  
with dawn like ashes on the blind:  
the house, the name, the honored grave—  
not one was worth the shame.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Imitate Edgar Lee Masters with a first-person graveyard confession about bribery, railroad interests, social ambition, daughters, whispers, and final disillusionment.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Edgar Lee Masters’ exact style, but here’s an original graveyard confession in the vein of an early-20th-century epitaphic free-verse monologue:

---

I was chairman of the county board,  
And my name was painted on the bank window  
In gold leaf.  
Men took off their hats to me on the square,  
And my wife sat straight in the front pew  
As if the sermon had been prepared  
For families such as ours.

The railroad men came first in overcoats,  
With gloves soft as a woman’s cheek,  
Talking of progress, grain shipments,  
New depots, rising land,  
And the future of the town.  
They left no money on the table—  
They were not crude men—  
But a note came later,  
And a contract for stone,  
And shares in the company  
Placed where my signature would not show.

I told myself the town would prosper.  
I told myself every great man  
Must understand the machinery of things.  
A road must go somewhere,  
And if it cut through widow Bell’s orchard  
Or left old Mercer’s store  
A mile from the new station,  
Was that my fault?  
Had I laid the iron with my own hands?

My daughters learned French in St. Louis.  
They came home with white gloves,  
With music, with opinions,  
With a shame of their father’s boots  
And their mother’s stories.  
I bought them a piano  
From money I called a dividend.  
I watched them move through rooms  
Bright with lamps and visiting lawyers,  
And thought:  
Now the family is lifted.

But the town had ears.  
It heard the wheels at midnight.  
It heard the clink inside the envelope.  
It heard the county maps unfolded  
Behind locked doors.  
Whispers passed from the barber’s chair  
To the druggist’s stove,  
From the church steps  
To the cemetery gate:  
He sold the south road.  
He took railroad money.  
He ruined Bell.  
He bought gentility.

When I died,  
The paper called me public-spirited.  
The minister spoke of enterprise.  
My daughters wore black veils  
And looked beautiful,  
Even in grief,  
Even in calculation.

Now I lie where no train stops,  
Beyond the sound of the whistle,  
Under a stone too large for truth.  
The grass has covered the old right-of-way.  
The depot burned.  
My daughters married men  
Who spent what I had hidden.  
And the town, which I tried to buy,  
Remembers me only  
When rain sinks the earth a little  
Over my grave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
